name: Vortioxetine (Trintellix)
summary: Once-daily antidepressant for major depression. Usually starts helping within 1-2 weeks, with bigger gains over 4-6 weeks. Watch closely for mood worsening or suicidal thoughts early on—especially ages 18-24.
description: Trintellix (vortioxetine) is a once-daily antidepressant used for major depressive disorder (unipolar). It works by increasing serotonin signaling in a few different ways (not just reuptake blockade). Many people notice early shifts in mood, energy, or thinking within 1-2 weeks, with fuller benefit by 4-6 weeks. The most common side effect is nausea. Like all antidepressants, it can temporarily increase suicidal thoughts in some younger patients, and it can trigger mania in people with bipolar disorder—so screening and close monitoring matter.
patient_summary: Trintellix is a once-daily antidepressant for major depression. Some people feel subtle improvements in 1-2 weeks, but the real change usually builds over 4-6 weeks. Nausea is the big one early. If you're 18-24 or have a history of bipolar symptoms, you need closer monitoring—because antidepressants can sometimes make things worse before they get better.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Antidepressant, Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor/5-HT1A Receptor Partial Agonist; Serotonin 5-HT3 Receptor Antagonist; Serotonin Modulator

linked_conditions.context: FDA-approved for major depressive disorder (unipolar). Usually dosed once daily and adjusted based on response and tolerability.
Often considered when depression includes prominent “brain fog” complaints (attention, processing speed, executive function), since its serotonergic receptor profile is different from standard SSRIs.

contraindications: Hypersensitivity to vortioxetine or any component of the formulation (including angioedema/anaphylaxis history)
Concomitant use of MAOIs intended to treat psychiatric disorders
Use of psychiatric MAOI within 14 days before starting vortioxetine
Starting an MAOI intended to treat psychiatric disorders within 21 days after stopping vortioxetine
Initiation of vortioxetine in a patient receiving IV methylene blue

efficacy_response.patient_text: Some people notice early changes within 1-2 weeks (like slightly better energy, less emotional heaviness, or clearer thinking). The bigger mood shift typically builds over 4-6 weeks.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Oral absorption with prolonged time to peak
pharmacokinetics.onset: Initial antidepressant effects may be noticed within 1-2 weeks; continued improvement through 4-6 weeks
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic oxidation primarily via CYP2D6 (major) with subsequent glucuronidation to inactive metabolites
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Can be taken without regard to meals

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Trintellix is used to treat {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:major depressive disorder (unipolar depression)}. It’s a once-daily antidepressant that builds over weeks—not a “take it and feel it in an hour” medication. In psychiatry, the main reason to pick vortioxetine is straightforward: depression symptoms, especially when people also complain about mental fog, low motivation, and emotional heaviness.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Major Depressive Disorder (MDD)}: Ongoing low mood and/or loss of interest, plus symptoms like low energy, sleep/appetite changes, guilt, concentration problems, or suicidal thoughts

sections.heading: What People Feel
sections.intro: This isn’t instant relief. Most people describe it as a slow turn of the dimmer switch over a few weeks. Here’s what tends to come up:

quotes: It wasn’t a miracle, but I felt a little more functional by week two.
My mood wasn’t “happy,” but I stopped feeling like I was drowning 24/7.
I noticed the brain fog eased before the sadness fully lifted.
The nausea was annoying at first, then it chilled out.
I had to take it with a small snack for the first couple weeks.
It wasn’t unbearable, but it was the main thing I noticed early.
items.note: Nausea is the most common side effect and is often worst during the first 1-2 weeks.

quotes: Compared to my last SSRI, this was way better sexually.
I still had some libido issues, but it didn’t feel like a total shutdown.
It wasn’t zero side effects, just less brutal than what I’d been on.
items.note: Rates of treatment-emergent sexual dysfunction can be lower than many SSRIs for some people, but it can still happen.

items.category: Activation / agitation (watch this closely early on)
quotes: I felt wired and restless after a dose increase.
My anxiety popped up during the first week before it settled.
I got more energy before my mood improved—which was uncomfortable.
items.note: Any new agitation, insomnia, impulsivity, panic, or mood worsening—especially in the first weeks or after dose changes—should be treated as a “call your prescriber” situation.

quotes: I suddenly felt too good—like not normal good—and I wasn’t sleeping.
My brain sped up, I got impulsive, and it didn’t feel like ‘recovery.’
It made me realize I might have bipolar tendencies.
items.note: Antidepressants can trigger hypomania/mania in people with bipolar disorder or bipolar risk—screening matters.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Trintellix works gradually. You’re not supposed to feel it like a sedative. Think weeks, not hours.
key_points: 1-2 weeks: Early changes may show up (slightly better energy, thinking, or less emotional heaviness)
4-6 weeks: Bigger and more reliable improvement typically shows up here
66 hours: Long half-life (it hangs around), which can make missed doses less dramatic than short half-life antidepressants

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: For most people, the question isn’t “does it work today?” It’s “is my baseline getting better over the next month?” If Trintellix is going to help, you usually see at least some movement by week 2-4, with continued improvement through week 6. If you’re at a therapeutic dose and nothing is changing by week 6-8, it may not be the right fit—or something else needs adjusting.

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: If depression suddenly worsens, or suicidal thoughts intensify—especially early in treatment or after dose changes—treat that as urgent and contact your clinician right away.
sections.black_box: Antidepressants increased the risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients in short-term studies. Closely monitor all antidepressant-treated patients for clinical worsening, and for emergence of suicidal thoughts and behaviors. Vortioxetine is not approved for use in pediatric patients.
other: Screen for bipolar disorder before starting: antidepressants can trigger mania/hypomania in vulnerable people
Serotonin syndrome risk (rare): higher risk when combined with other serotonergic meds or MAOIs
Bleeding risk: serotonergic antidepressants can increase bleeding risk, especially with NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets, or anticoagulants
Hyponatremia/SIADH risk (rare but real): more likely in older adults, people on diuretics, or those with low baseline sodium
Narrow-angle glaucoma risk in susceptible individuals due to mild pupillary dilation
CNS effects: dizziness, abnormal dreams, cognitive slowing in some people—be cautious with driving until you know your response
Seizures reported rarely; use caution if seizure risk is present
patient_counseling: If you’re 18-24 (or have a history of suicidal thoughts), plan on closer follow-up early on.
Tell your prescriber immediately if you notice new or worsening: agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia, hypomania/mania, or suicidal thinking.
Avoid combining with MAOIs. There are required washout windows (see interactions section).
If you take NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen), aspirin, or blood thinners, ask about bleeding risk—especially if you bruise easily or have GI bleeding history.
Know serotonin syndrome red flags: agitation/confusion, sweating, tremor, muscle stiffness, diarrhea, fever—seek urgent care if severe.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common: nausea. Also possible: constipation/diarrhea, dizziness, dry mouth, abnormal dreams, itching. Sexual side effects can happen, but may be less intense than many SSRIs for some people.
plain_language_list: Nausea (the big one—often early and dose-related)
Sexual side effects (can happen in any direction: desire, arousal, orgasm)

common.patient_note: This is the headline side effect. It often shows up early and may improve over 1-2 weeks. Some people do better taking it with food or at a consistent time each day.
Usually mild, but it can mess with driving or workouts at first. If you feel off-balance, slow down and reassess after a week or two.
Can be part of the early GI adjustment. If it’s severe, persistent, or you’re getting dehydrated, it’s a medical issue—not something to tough out.
Hydration, fiber, and routine movement help. If constipation becomes significant, address it early rather than waiting.
Annoying but manageable—water, sugar-free gum, and good dental care matter if it persists.
Some people get vivid dreams or weird sleep texture. If it’s disrupting sleep, timing the dose earlier in the day can help for some people.

serious: Suicidal thoughts/behaviors (especially ages 18-24 early in treatment or after dose changes): urgent clinical follow-up needed
Mania/hypomania (rare): decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, unusually elevated or irritable mood—stop and contact prescriber urgently
Serotonin syndrome (rare but potentially life-threatening): agitation/confusion, tremor, rigidity, fever, sweating, diarrhea, seizures—emergency evaluation
Hyponatremia/SIADH (rare): headache, confusion, weakness, falls, seizures—especially in older adults or those on diuretics
Bleeding complications (risk increased with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants): easy bruising, nosebleeds, black stools, vomiting blood—urgent evaluation

sections.heading: Critical Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Trintellix has important serotonin-related interaction rules (especially MAOIs). It’s also metabolized mainly through CYP2D6, so genetics and drug interactions can affect dosing.

items.with: MAOIs used for psychiatric disorders (and related serotonin-toxicity risk agents)
items.risk: Contraindicated. High risk of serotonin syndrome.
items.action: Wait 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting vortioxetine. Wait 21 days after stopping vortioxetine before starting an MAOI (consider longer—up to 32 days—in severe obesity due to prolonged half-life).

items.with: Other serotonergic meds (SSRIs/SNRIs, TCAs, triptans, tramadol, fentanyl, methadone, meperidine, lithium, buspirone, amphetamines, St John’s wort, tryptophan)
items.risk: Increased serotonin syndrome risk, especially when stacking multiple agents.
items.action: Avoid unnecessary combinations. If combination is intentional, use the lowest effective doses and educate on serotonin syndrome symptoms.

items.with: NSAIDs, aspirin, antiplatelets, anticoagulants (eg, warfarin, DOACs)
items.risk: Increased bleeding risk due to impaired platelet aggregation.
items.action: Use caution and monitor for bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding symptoms. Consider gastroprotection if clinically appropriate and risk is high.

items.with: CYP2D6 considerations (poor metabolizers or strong CYP2D6 inhibitors)
items.risk: Higher vortioxetine exposure may increase side effects.
items.action: In known CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, maximum recommended dose is 10 mg/day. If side effects spike after adding interacting meds, reassess dose.

items.risk: Additive CNS effects (dizziness, impaired alertness) in some people.
items.action: Use caution. Don’t assume you’re safe to drive until you know how you respond.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Trintellix has a relatively long half-life, so many people have fewer discontinuation symptoms than with shorter half-life antidepressants. Still: don’t wing it. If you’ve been on it for at least 2 weeks, you and your prescriber can either taper over 1-2 weeks or stop more directly depending on dose, history, and sensitivity.
key_points: If treatment has lasted <2 weeks: tapering usually isn’t necessary
If treatment has lasted ≥2 weeks: taper over 1-2 weeks OR consider direct stop, since discontinuation syndrome risk is low-to-moderate
If tapering from ≥15 mg/day: step down to 10 mg/day for 1 week before stopping
If you’ve had withdrawal problems before, are on a higher dose, or feel sensitive: taper slower (eg, over 4 weeks)
Some people on long-term treatment (>6 months) and with discontinuation history may do best with a very slow taper (>3 months)
If withdrawal symptoms become intolerable: go back to the last stable dose and taper more gradually

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Trintellix is taken once daily and adjusted slowly based on response and side effects. The goal is to land on the lowest dose that actually helps—without you feeling wrecked by nausea or activation.

adult.mdd_titration: Increase by 5 to 10 mg/day at ≥1-week intervals based on response and tolerability
adult.cyp2d6_poor_metabolizer_max: Maximum 10 mg/day in known CYP2D6 poor metabolizers
adult.administration: Take once daily, with or without food

sections.simple_explanation: Most people start at 5-10 mg daily, then move up in weekly steps if needed. The max is usually 20 mg/day, but some people (especially known CYP2D6 poor metabolizers) shouldn’t go above 10 mg/day.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups
sections.text: Depression during pregnancy and postpartum is high-stakes. Decisions should be shared, individualized, and based on severity, relapse history, and what has actually worked for the patient before. Vortioxetine isn’t usually the first pick for someone treatment-naïve in pregnancy, but people who are stable and functioning on it may continue depending on risk/benefit.
sections.pregnancy: Data specific to vortioxetine in pregnancy are limited. As a serotonergic antidepressant with SSRI-like properties, late-pregnancy exposure in the SSRI class is associated with neonatal adaptation syndrome (usually resolves within ~2 weeks) and a rare risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Stopping or lowering antidepressants right before delivery to “prevent” neonatal symptoms is generally not recommended because relapse risk is real and untreated depression carries its own risks (preterm birth, low birth weight, preeclampsia, postpartum depression, impaired bonding). Use the lowest effective dose of a single agent, optimize dosing before switching, and monitor monthly with a validated tool when possible. Encourage enrollment in the National Pregnancy Registry for Antidepressants when eligible.
sections.lactation: Vortioxetine is present in breast milk. Available reports suggest low infant exposure (relative infant dose roughly ~1% to ~2% in limited data). Breastfeeding may be reasonable in some cases, but monitoring matters: watch infant sleep, feeding, irritability, and growth. If starting a new antidepressant postpartum in a breastfeeding, treatment-naïve patient, another agent may be preferred depending on clinical context.
sections.pediatrics: Not approved for use in pediatric patients. Antidepressants carry an increased risk of suicidal thoughts/behaviors in children, adolescents, and young adults; close monitoring is required.
sections.geriatrics: US labeling refers to adult dosing. In older adults, SSRIs and similar serotonergic antidepressants are used with caution due to SIADH/hyponatremia risk and fall risk from dizziness. Consider starting at the lower end of dosing and monitor sodium closely during initiation and dose changes, especially in patients ≥65 or on diuretics.
sections.renal: No dosage adjustment necessary for any degree of kidney impairment. Unlikely to be significantly dialyzed; no supplemental dosing needed with hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, CRRT, or PIRRT.

sections.heading: Clinical Monitoring
items: Depression severity and function: track mood, motivation, sleep, appetite, cognition, work/school function, relationships, and daily functioning
Suicidal ideation and behavior: especially at the beginning of therapy and during dose increases/decreases; involve family/caregiver observation when appropriate
Activation symptoms: anxiety, agitation, panic attacks, insomnia, irritability, hostility, impulsivity, akathisia—especially early on
Mania/hypomania: decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, risky behavior, unusually elevated/irritable mood—screen before starting and reassess if symptoms emerge
Serotonin syndrome: mental status changes, autonomic instability, neuromuscular findings, GI symptoms; higher vigilance when combined with other serotonergic agents

Hyponatremia/SIADH: monitor for confusion, weakness, headache, falls; check sodium in higher-risk patients (older adults, low body weight, on diuretics, prior hyponatremia) especially after starting or dose changes
Bleeding: bruising, nosebleeds, GI bleeding signs (black stools, vomiting blood), especially with NSAIDs/aspirin/anticoagulants
Adverse effects burden: nausea severity, dizziness, sleep changes, sexual functioning, and adherence
Drug interaction review: reassess when adding serotonergic meds, anticoagulants/NSAIDs, or when MAOI exposure is possible

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Trintellix is only available as oral tablets in standard strengths. It’s taken once daily, and you adjust the dose slowly to find the sweet spot between benefit and side effects.

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Vortioxetine is a serotonin modulator. It increases serotonin signaling by blocking serotonin reuptake and also directly interacting with several serotonin receptors. In plain terms: it doesn’t just “raise serotonin”—it changes how serotonin networks communicate, which is why it can feel different from a standard SSRI for some people.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: Trintellix is a reasonable option for unipolar major depression, especially when someone hasn’t tolerated or hasn’t benefited from a first-line SSRI/SNRI—or when cognitive symptoms (“brain fog”) are part of the depression picture. It is not used as a PRN anxiety med, not a sedative, and not a rapid tranquilizer. If bipolar disorder is on the table, don’t use it as monotherapy—screen carefully and treat mood stability first.

seo.title: Vortioxetine (Trintellix): Uses, Dosing, Side Effects & Safety
seo.description: Trintellix (vortioxetine) for major depressive disorder: once-daily dosing (5-20 mg), when it starts working (1-2 weeks, builds to 4-6 weeks), common side effects (nausea), boxed warning on suicidality in young adults, serotonin syndrome risk, MAOI washout rules, and safe discontinuation.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and verified against FDA prescribing information, APA clinical practice guidelines, and current peer-reviewed literature.

faqs.a: Trintellix (vortioxetine) is used to treat major depressive disorder (unipolar depression). It’s not a PRN medication for anxiety or panic, and it’s not meant to work instantly. It’s a daily antidepressant that builds over weeks.

faqs.q: How long does Trintellix take to work?
faqs.a: Some people notice early shifts in 1-2 weeks (energy, mental clarity, less heaviness). Bigger improvement usually builds over 4-6 weeks. If nothing is changing by 6-8 weeks at a therapeutic dose, it may not be the right fit or the plan may need adjustment.

faqs.q: What dose of Trintellix is typical?
faqs.a: Most adults start at 5 to 10 mg once daily. If needed, the dose can be increased by 5 to 10 mg at weekly (or slower) intervals, up to 20 mg/day (usual max). In known CYP2D6 poor metabolizers, the max is 10 mg/day.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects?
faqs.a: Nausea is the most common side effect (and often the one people complain about early). Other possible side effects include constipation or diarrhea, dizziness, dry mouth, and abnormal dreams. Sexual side effects can happen, but some people find them less intense than with other SSRIs.

faqs.q: Does Trintellix cause sexual side effects?
faqs.a: It can. In studies and real-world use, some people report lower rates compared to many SSRIs, but it’s not guaranteed. If sexual function changes, talk to your clinician—dose changes, timing, or switching strategies can help.

faqs.q: Is Trintellix linked to suicidal thoughts?
faqs.a: All antidepressants carry a boxed warning: in short-term studies, there was an increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviors in pediatric and young adult patients. People ages 18-24 need close monitoring early in treatment and during dose changes. In adults over 24, short-term studies did not show increased risk; in adults 65 and older, risk appeared decreased. Regardless of age, any sudden worsening or suicidality should be treated as urgent.

Yes—rarely, but it can happen, especially if someone has bipolar disorder or bipolar risk that wasn’t recognized yet. Red flags include decreased need for sleep, racing thoughts, impulsivity, and unusually elevated or irritable mood. Screening for bipolar disorder before starting is important.

faqs.q: Can I take Trintellix with an MAOI?
faqs.a: No. It’s contraindicated. You need washout windows: wait 14 days after stopping an MAOI before starting vortioxetine, and wait 21 days after stopping vortioxetine before starting an MAOI (longer may be considered in severe obesity).

faqs.q: Do I need to taper off Trintellix?
faqs.a: Often you can taper over 1-2 weeks if you’ve been on it ≥2 weeks, and some people can stop more directly because discontinuation risk is relatively low-to-moderate. If you’re on 15 mg/day or higher, one taper approach is dropping to 10 mg/day for a week before stopping. If you’ve had antidepressant withdrawal before or you’re sensitive, taper slower.

faqs.q: Is Trintellix safe in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Data specific to vortioxetine are limited. Treatment decisions should be individualized because untreated depression in pregnancy has real risks, and stopping effective medication can cause relapse. For breastfeeding, vortioxetine appears in breast milk, but limited data suggest low infant exposure; infants should still be monitored for sleep, feeding, irritability, and growth. This should be a shared decision with your clinician.

faqs.q: Does Trintellix help anxiety or insomnia?
faqs.a: It’s not primarily an anxiety PRN medication and it isn’t a sleep medication. If your anxiety is part of depression, improving depression can indirectly help. Early on, some people feel more activated or restless, and sleep can temporarily worsen—so monitoring and adjusting the plan matters.
